Read the transcript of the audio guide
  1. In January 1936, in a New Jersey courthouse, the most famous scientist in the world put his name to a government form declaring that he meant to become an American. source
  2. Einstein was born in Ulm, in the kingdom of Württemberg, in 1879, and grew up in Munich. source
  3. In 1905, working as a clerk in the Swiss patent office in Bern, he published the papers that remade physics. source
  4. Einstein held professorships in Zurich, Prague and Berlin, and in 1921 he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. source
  5. Einstein was abroad — lecturing in the United States — when Hitler became chancellor in January 1933. source
  6. He resigned from the Prussian Academy of Sciences, gave up his German citizenship, and resolved not to return. source
  7. In a public statement that March he set the condition under which he would live anywhere: source
  8. As long as I have any choice, I will only stay in a country where political liberty, toleration, and equality of all citizens before the law are the rule. source
  9. The Institute for Advanced Study, a new research centre in Princeton, had offered him a post. source
  10. On 15 January 1936, Einstein filed his Declaration of Intention — an immigrant's sworn "first papers," the formal statement that he meant to become a citizen. source
  11. He took the oath of citizenship in 1940, keeping the Swiss citizenship he had held since young adulthood, so that he ended his life a citizen of two republics and no empire. source
  12. He used his fame as an American deliberately: for refugees fleeing the same Europe he had escaped, for civil rights, and against the misuse of the physics he had helped create. source
  13. If you had to choose a country to live in, what would it need to promise you?
Read the transcript of the short and the video
  1. Albert Einstein left Germany in 1933 as the Nazis came to power, and never went back. source
  2. He settled at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, filed his first citizenship papers in 1936, and took the oath as an American in 1940 — one of the few immigrants whose surname became a byword for genius. source
  3. In 1905, working as a clerk in the Swiss patent office in Bern, he published the papers that remade physics. source
  4. Einstein held professorships in Zurich, Prague and Berlin, and in 1921 he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics. source
  5. He used his fame as an American deliberately: for refugees fleeing the same Europe he had escaped, for civil rights, and against the misuse of the physics he had helped create. source
  6. Read the full story, with every source, on this page.
